title: Memory guides
intro: Short, safe steps that help games run smoothly when RAM is tight. Each guide says what to check first, so you only change what needs changing.

guides.title: Run your RAM at its rated speed (XMP or EXPO)
guides.summary: Most RAM kits run at a slow default speed until you turn on their profile in the BIOS.
steps: Open Task Manager (Ctrl+Shift+Esc), go to Performance > Memory and look at Speed.
Compare it with the speed on your RAM kit's label or product page, for example 6000 MT/s.
If Task Manager shows less, restart into your BIOS and turn on the memory profile: XMP on most Intel boards, EXPO or DOCP on most AMD boards. Save and restart.
Play for a while. If the PC crashes, freezes or won't start, go back into the BIOS and pick a lower profile, or load the default settings.
guides.note: Some tools, such as CPU-Z, show half the number (3000 MHz for a 6000 MT/s kit). That's the same speed, shown a different way.

guides.title: Use two sticks in the right slots
guides.summary: One stick of RAM runs in single channel, which can cost real FPS in CPU-heavy games.
steps: Open Task Manager > Performance > Memory and look at Slots used, for example 2 of 4.
If you have one stick, a matching pair is the better setup for gaming.
On a board with four slots, two sticks usually go in the second and fourth slots counted from the CPU, often labeled A2 and B2. Check your motherboard manual to be sure.
Four sticks give you more RAM but can stop it from reaching its rated speed, especially with DDR5.
guides.note: Turn the PC off and unplug it before you move RAM.

guides.title: Check whether you're running out of RAM
guides.summary: When RAM fills up, Windows moves data to disk and games stutter.
steps: Start your game, then open Task Manager > Performance > Memory.
If In use is close to your total RAM, or Committed is close to its limit, you're running out.
Close apps you don't need while you play, or see the background apps guide below.
16 GB is the minimum for current games. 32 GB is the comfortable amount if you stream, keep a browser open or play large open-world games.
If memory use keeps climbing over days without a reason, restart the PC.
guides.note: Low Free memory on its own is normal. See the Standby memory guide.

guides.title: Calm background apps while you play
guides.summary: Browsers, launchers and chat apps keep using RAM and CPU while you play.
steps: Close what you don't need before you start a game.
For apps you keep open, use Games & processes > Background apps. It can lower their priority and memory priority, so Windows keeps your game's memory first when RAM runs low.

On Intel CPUs with E-cores, or AMD Ryzen CPUs with two CCDs, the Background apps preset can keep background apps at Normal priority and move them to the E-cores or the second CCD. Your game can still use every core; only the background apps are limited.
In your browser, turn on Memory Saver (Chrome) or Sleeping tabs (Edge) so idle tabs give memory back.
guides.note: Memory priority doesn't limit how much RAM an app can use. It decides whose memory Windows takes back first when RAM runs short.

guides.title: Keep the page file on
guides.summary: The page file lets Windows handle memory spikes. Turning it off can crash games even on PCs with lots of RAM.
steps: Press Win+R, type sysdm.cpl and press Enter.
Go to Advanced > Performance Settings > Advanced > Virtual memory > Change.
Make sure Automatically manage paging file size for all drives is ticked.
If you set a custom size before, switch back to automatic unless you have a specific reason.
guides.note: If you can, keep the page file on your fastest SSD.

guides.title: Understand Standby memory and memory cleaners
guides.summary: Windows keeps recently used files in spare RAM so they load faster. It gives that memory back the moment a program needs it.
steps: In Task Manager > Performance > Memory, Cached is mostly Standby memory, and Standby memory counts as Available.
Low Free memory is normal and isn't a problem by itself.
Memory cleaner apps that empty the cache usually make things slower afterwards, because Windows has to read those files from disk again.
Only clear Standby memory if you've measured stutter that goes away right after clearing it.
guides.note: Available memory is the number that matters. Free memory isn't.

guides.title: Know what Memory Integrity costs
guides.summary: Memory Integrity (Core isolation) and virtualization-based security protect your PC but can lower FPS in some games.
steps: Check it in Windows Security > Device security > Core isolation details.
The FPS preset on the Windows tweaks page explains the trade-off and can turn these features off. Read its warnings before you use it.
Some anti-cheat systems check these settings. If a game won't start afterwards, undo the preset.
guides.note: Don't turn these off on a PC you use for banking, work or school.
